newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Japan stocks seen wavering, gains capped.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Japan stocks seen wavering, gains capped.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are expected to be pressured this week by Friday's sharp fall on Wall Street with the Nikkei average possibly testing the year's closing low, brokers said.
Selling in the banking sector would continue, they said.

"Nikkei futures will probably react to the Dow fall and weaken the Nikkei average enough for it to test the January 10 closing low of 17,303," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities Co. Ltd. "As seen in the previous week, banking sector shares are weak due to dissolution of cross share-holdings and such selling is likely to continue but some investors will buy laggard low-priced stocks backed by firm earnings forecasts regardless of how the indices are and regardless of how market sentiment is."
Renewed inflation and interest rate concerns sent Wall Street stocks tumbling 148 points or 2.3 percent on Friday to 6,392, the Dow's eighth steepest fall ever.
"There is still much dissolution of cross share-holdings left and bank shares especially are likely to be to weakened by it," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
"Until the bank shares stop slipping, the market will keep an eye on the January 10 closing low of 17,303," Ueki said.
Brokers said Nippon Credit Bank Ltd would be in the spotlight after ending limit high on Friday in response to an announcement it would tie up with Bankers Trust New York Corp.

"It was mostly margin trade-related short covering on Friday, but somewhere along the way, investors may gradually start to commend the (tie-up) move as it means there is one less possible factor to upset Japan's financial system," said Akishige Ishikura, an analyst at Dai-Ichi Securities.

On Friday, NCB inspired a flood of buy-backs in the banking sector, boosting the 225-share Nikkei average to close up 361.23 points, or 2.07 percent, at 17,846.98. But that was little changed from the April 4 close of 17,860.59.
Brokers said the last-minute uplift, which was also helped by bargain-hunting pension funds buying blue chips, had buoyed sentiment.
"If public funds continue to trickle into the market in moments of weakness, fears of sharp falls could be eased," one broker said.

Further faltering of the yen against the dollar, which at one point in the previous week sent the yen below 127, would help prop up the market, as it would inspire buying of export-strong shares, brokers said.
But they added that the some of the recent high-flyers were losing momentum to profit-taking and it remained to be seen if investors would continue to show interest in smaller shares.
"Investors are starting to trade exporter issues based on technical factors rather than the weak yen, so some are being bought while others sold," said Toyo Securities director Haruo Nakaharu.
Brokers added that buying was detected in low-priced, domestic-demand sensitive issues such as steel and chemicals, and this was likely to continue in the coming week.

"Portfolio reshuffling is bound to continue for some time and some of the financial sector shares which are being sold are being replaced by such raw material shares," Nikko's Ueki said. "But those shares do not affect the indices much, so although trade may be active, the indices could be soft."
